extracted.intended_audience: the higher and middle classes; lay readers and parishioners interested in religion, morals, and the civic effects of commerce
extracted.subtask_description: A nineteenth-century lay sermon addressing how different forms of Christianity do or do not check the commercial spirit; it evaluates religious practice, preaching, learning, and discipline as antidotes to mercantile excess. The piece argues what kind of religion genuinely influences moral and civic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regeneration versus mere moral preliminaries
rubrics_metrics.description: To abstain from wrong and be industrious, useful, and of seemly bearing are preliminary conditions rather than the proper and peculiar effects of Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists Christianity's true effect is 'being born again' — an indispensable act/infusion (1 John iii; St John) — not merely external morality or decorous conduct. Superficial moral behaviour alone does not equal the transforming power Christianity claims to produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion must engage the understanding and affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion should employ and occupy the understandings of men and combine their affections with it as a system of truth gradually manifesting itself to the intellect as well as a system of motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If religion is only 'plain and easy' it leaves the understanding vacant and available for worldly pursuits. Effective religion must assimilate both intellect and feeling so that faith is not merely an external assent but an inward, reflective possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and learning in preaching and theological works
rubrics_metrics.description: Sermons and theological writings should present 'more thoughts, more facts and images, more excitements to inquiry and intellectual effort' than superficial addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Dr. Donne and Jeremy Taylor and the long learned folios of earlier centuries as models; substantive, learned preaching that fixes minds is contrasted with modern short, facile sermons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological education and trained ministry are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious bodies should provide for ministers specially trained and educated for the ministry; omission of such training impoverishes theological learning among adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a critique, the Society of Friends (Quakers) are noted for excluding ordained/educated ministers, resulting in less theological learning despite worldly shrewdness; this limits religion's intellectual force as a counterweight to commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church discipline and communal enforcement of confessed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of discipline that connects church members and enforces confessed principles is an important guard against worldly vanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Friends' 'orderly and beneficent Society' and its effective discipline are praised as preserving decency and philanthropy, even if their theology is unstudied; discipline helps sustain moral habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion must act as a counterpoise to the spirit of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: For religion to check the excesses of commerce it must have adequate countervailing power — not merely private decency but a principle that resists the valuation of everything by marketable worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contends the commercial spirit estimates all pursuits by market value; only a religion that occupies mind and motive can resist that tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious seriousness evidenced by controversy and doctrinal engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The warmth, frequency, and public engagement in religious controversies are symptomatic of a religion's depth and seriousness among a people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier periods' intense polemical literature and learned disputation (even if sometimes excessive) are cited as signs that religion then occupied men's minds; modern toleration may indicate comparative indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural distribution must be accompanied by learning and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributing the Bible 'and the Bible only' among the poor without notes or comment is inadequate; Scripture requires learned exposition to address difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bishop's slogan 'No notes! No comment!' is criticized as either ignorant or fanatical; the text argues for the necessity of learned interpretation and comment to yield new fruits of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion cannot be resigned to clergy by the laity
rubrics_metrics.description: When many in society 'resign' religion to the clergyman of the parish and only 'pray and bear by proxy,' religion ceases to be an active personal force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author distinguishes between respectful observance and real inward religion; passive reliance on clergy correlates with the laity's preoccupation with worldly business and diminishes religion's civic influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine observance (family prayer, Scripture reading) as an indicator but not a guarantor
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular family prayer and Scripture reading among respectable laity are marks of religious habit, but they may coexist with worldly avidity if not underpinned by intellectual and heartfelt faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of respectable laity who observe family worship and habits are given; the author warns such practices alone may be grafts (external) rather than fruits (internal regeneration).

rubrics_metrics.name: A faith made 'plain and easy' drains study and intellectual resistance to worldly aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianities that make all truths of Scripture 'so very manifest or so very easy' render study and research needless, leaving minds free for worldly pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This easy, uninquiring religion produces adherents who are shrewd and thriving in business because their understanding remains at leisure for temporal interests rather than being occupied by profound theological reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion should unite imaginative (poetic) and intellectual (philosophic) faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry tends to render devotees careless of money; philosophy inspires contempt of outward wealth; religion should unite the best of both to displace avarice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues religion is the 'poetry and philosophy of all mankind' and to effect moral change must call into action both imaginative and intellective powers as well as offer substantial objects for devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of ancient learning and classical philosophy as a civilizing check
rubrics_metrics.description: Education in classics and the thoughts of Plato, Aristotle, and the ancients cultivates virtues and habits of public life that counterbalance the spirit of barter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author laments the decline of reverence for ancient philosophy among the modern gentry and suggests that absorption in corporeal/object-based thinking predisposes men to value sensory/market goods over higher ends.
